scenes.say: Which items fill a four kilo backpack for the most value? The priciest item is not in the best answer. By the end you'll fill knapsack, L I S and L C S tables by hand.
Today you will do three things. Fill a knapsack table by hand. Build the longest increasing run with a tails list. And fill a grid for the longest common subsequence.
lines: Knapsack: take or leave, by hand

scenes.title: 0/1 knapsack
scenes.statement: Each item is taken once or left. Maximize value within the weight limit.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. For example, weights one, three, four, capacity four. The best value is thirty five.

scenes.head: Backpack: 4 kg, three items
scenes.say: Item A weighs one kilo and is worth fifteen dollars. Item B, three kilos, twenty. Item C, four kilos, thirty. Each is taken or left, never split. Grabbing the priciest, C, fills the bag: thirty. But A and B together weigh four kilos and give thirty five.

scenes.head: dp over capacity, item by item
scenes.say: Let dp of c be the best value at capacity c. All start at zero. Item A: one kilo, fifteen dollars. Every capacity from one up can hold it, so all become fifteen. Item B: three kilos, twenty. Capacity three becomes twenty. Capacity four takes B plus A's last kilo: thirty five. Item C: four kilos, thirty. That's less than thirty five, so nothing changes.

scenes.head: Knapsack in six lines
scenes.say: In code, one array over capacity. For each item, loop capacity from the top down, and ask: better to leave the item, or take it plus the best of what's left? It prints thirty five. Cost is items times capacity: pseudo-polynomial, since capacity is a value.
Your turn. Only item A, one kilo, fifteen dollars, capacity four. This time the capacity loop runs upward, from one to four. What does dp of four end up as? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: One item (1 kg, $15), c loops 1 up to 4. dp[4]?

scenes.head: Trap: capacity loop upward
scenes.say: Sixty. Upward, dp of one is fifteen. Then dp of two reuses that cell: thirty. Then forty five, then sixty. One item, used four times. Downward avoids it.

panels.label: bug

scenes.title: Longest increasing subsequence
scenes.statement: Keep the order, skip freely. Find the longest strictly rising run.
scenes.say: New problem. For example, ten, nine, two, five, three, seven, one hundred one, eighteen. Longest rising run? Four.

scenes.head: Longest increasing subsequence
scenes.say: Look at the array. Two, then three, then seven, then eighteen: each bigger than the last. Length four. Nothing longer exists.

scenes.head: Beat n squared with tails
scenes.say: The classic follow-up: can you beat n squared? The simple table looks back at every earlier number. The trick is a list called tails. Slot k holds the smallest end of any rising run of length k plus one. Smaller ends are easier to extend.

scenes.head: Tails: first four numbers
scenes.say: Keep the list tails. Ten arrives, so tails is ten. Nine arrives, smaller, so it replaces ten. Two arrives, smaller again: it replaces nine. Five arrives, bigger than all: it extends the list.

scenes.head: Tails: the last four numbers
scenes.say: Three arrives and replaces five: two, three is a better start than two, five. Seven arrives, bigger than all: it extends. One hundred one extends again. Eighteen arrives and replaces one hundred one. Four slots are used, so the answer is four.

scenes.head: LIS with binary search
scenes.say: In code, lower bound finds the first tail not smaller than x. None found means x is bigger than all: append. Otherwise overwrite that tail. One binary search per number: O of n log n. On our array it prints four.
Your turn. Array four, one, five, two, six. Run the tails list by hand. How long is tails at the end? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: tails for 4, 1, 5, 2, 6
scenes.say: Three. Four starts the list. One replaces four. Five extends it. Two replaces five. Six extends it: one, two, six. Length three.

scenes.head: Three LIS traps
scenes.say: Tails isn't the run. For three, five, one it ends as one, five. Only its length is real. Equal values? Lower bound is strict, upper bound allows equals. The simple table is O of n squared.

scenes.title: Longest common subsequence
scenes.statement: Find the longest sequence that appears, in order, in both strings.
scenes.say: Last problem. Two strings, A B C B D A B and B D C A B A. Longest common subsequence? Four.

cues.example: A B C B D A B

scenes.head: Two strings, one grid
scenes.say: Diff tools compare files this way. Take two strings, A B C B D A B and B D C A B A. A subsequence skips letters but keeps order. Longest common has length four. Cell i j holds the answer for the first i and first j letters.

items.label: string 1
items.cue: A B C B D A B

items.label: string 2
items.cue: B D C A B A

scenes.head: LCS grid: rows A and B
scenes.say: Now the grid. Rows are the letters of A B C B D A B, columns are B D C A B A. The border is zero: an empty string shares nothing. Row A against B, D, C: no match, so zero. Then A meets A: a match, so diagonal plus one makes one. The rest stays one. Row B: B meets B, a match: one. The rest follows the same rule.

scenes.head: The grid in code
scenes.say: Same rule in code, with a zero border. If the letters match, take the diagonal plus one. Otherwise take the better of above and left. The corner prints four. Cost: n times m.

scenes.head: LCS grid: rows C, B, D
scenes.say: Row C: the C against C match gives two. Row B: two matches, reaching three. Row D: one match, D against D. Each cell reads only above, left, and diagonal.

scenes.head: LCS grid: the last rows
scenes.say: Row A: A meets A, and the row builds up to four. Row B: B matches too. The corner holds four. One common subsequence is B C B A.
Your turn. Two short strings: A B C and A C B. What is the length of their longest common subsequence? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: ABC vs ACB
scenes.say: Two. A B is in order in both. So is A C. But B and C come in opposite orders, so all three can't fit.

scenes.head: Three LCS follow-ups
scenes.say: Memory: keep two rows. Off by one: cell i j compares letters i minus one and j minus one. Substring can't skip letters, subsequence can.
rows: two rows: each needs only the one above

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Knapsack? A dp over capacity, loop capacity downward, items times capacity. L I S? Tails with binary search, O of n log n. L C S? A grid: match, diagonal plus one, otherwise best of above, left. Mistake? Capacity upward.
rows: dp over capacity, loop downward, n × cap
tails + binary search, O(n log n)
capacity loop upward reuses an item

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these three next. LeetCode four sixteen, Partition Equal Subset Sum, is knapsack. LeetCode three hundred, Longest Increasing Subsequence, is tails. LeetCode eleven forty three, Longest Common Subsequence, is the grid.
So say this. Knapsack: dp over capacity, take or leave each item, loop capacity downward. L I S: a tails list with binary search. L C S: a grid where a match means diagonal plus one.
lines: Knapsack: dp over capacity; loop it downward.
LIS: tails list + binary search, O(n log n).
LCS: grid; match = diagonal + 1, else max.
